While dealing with the [underlying flaw](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/113288) caused by joining two realtime streams across a buffer, this looks like it would produce seriously glitchy microphone audio because it jumps across large numbers of samples whenever a drift has been detected.  

The buffer under-run case is going to sound like a stutter when a short segment of audio gets repeated.  

The buffer over-run case is going to sound like a break where a segment of audio gets dropped.

Do you have recordings of what it sounds like when these occur?

I believe the buffer under-run case was "fixed" by PR #93200 by packing zeros into the stream when the buffer was exhausted, which is also not going to sound good.

Since the drift tends to be quite slow, we might get away with an algorithm that inserts or drops individual samples from the stream as it goes along to keep them in balance.  This isn't going to sound great either, when it happens, but the glitching would be a lot less.

In any case, I think these glitches should be counted instead of printed to the debug window.  I believe that's the reasoning behind the function [AudioEffectCapture.get_discarded_frames()](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_audioeffectcapture.html#class-audioeffectcapture-method-get-discarded-frames), so you have a programmatic way to tell that the sound data is corrupted, which is better than having to scan through the debug logs to find out.

Well, in my experience at least, the drift is gradual, and this patch only corrects it when it gets within a certain range of the current input_position.

That's fine with me. I just adapted the printed output that was already present in the code.

What is your use-case for playing back the microphone input to the audio system? If you're just looking to record it, are you aware that in 4.6, there is now a [new preferred method](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/113288) for capturing it?

> What is your use-case for playing back the microphone input to the audio system? If you're just looking to record it, are you aware that in 4.6, there is now a [new preferred method](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/113288) for capturing it?

I mean, I'm sure most people would find your listed method preferable because they are likely capturing the audio for multiplayer gaming. I personally just prefer to capture the audio at the Bus level so I can easily set up effects and position the audio before I capture it (I'm capturing the audio in an AudioEffect I made later in the bus and piping it to OBS for my streams).

Just to be clear, so you aren't actually playing it back on your own speakers?

Before I get ahead of myself, I'll clarify that we definitely _do want_ microphone playback to be as smooth as possible. So improvements in this regard are appreciated.
However, with https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/113288 merged, the use case for this has shrunk significantly, since most people do not actually want to play back the microphone sounds, they just want to capture it. If i understand it correctly, this is also the case for you, although you want to apply effects before capturing the audio.

This being said, I can imagine two alternative changes for your situation that would better solve the problem:

1. Apply effects in OBS (or another intermediate dedicated audio effects program) instead. This may be especially preferable because other programs may have more extensive capabilities of live audio manipulation, through VSTs etc.
2. Process audio on a 'capture pipeline' separately from the audio playback, driven by the microphone's clock instead of the speaker's clock. I'm not quite sure this would work, and it would require extensive discussion before this could be approached.

I'd say, regardless of whether you're OK with going with solution 1, we can continue to discuss this PR as the use-case will stay to be supported. But I think it's important to view it in context, especially with the concerns that goatchurch has brought up which might make it more difficult to improve the situation than just merging the PR.

Afaict, this code only improves the situation with the original microphone handling. I mean if AudioStreamPlaybackMicrophone is being deprecated altogether then I totally understand the reservation. As is, this code fixes what I believe to be flawed logic in the current implementation (which doesn't seem to treat the input buffer as a ring buffer when testing if it needs to correct for underrun) and let's the output position overrun the input position resulting in garbled audio eventually.

As far as the options presented, I was already planning on transitioning to a generic PulseAudioStreamPlayback class that I am finishing up to input audio from other apps, mics, whatever. So, I just figured the project would want this to just work, and did this in the interim.

Yea, that's totally fine. We do want to improve `AudioStreamPlaybackMicrophone`, so we'll continue to review the PR on its own merits (I personally haven't looked at the code yet. I just wanted to start with the context of the PR first).

The new function means that the logic of the `AudioStreamMicrophone` can be implemented in pure GDScript with an `AudioStreamGenerator`

```GDScript
func _process():
    var audio_samples: PackedVector2Array = AudioServer.get_input_frames(AudioServer.get_input_frames_available())
    $AudioStreamGenerator.get_stream_playback().push_buffer(audio_samples)
```

(Perhaps `AudioServer.get_input_frames(-1)` should return all available frames.)

Doing it this way, the lag between the microphone and audio output is about the same, because the `AudioStreamMicrophone` allows the buffer to run ahead for half its length at startup.

There is always going to be an unacceptable lag between the microphone and speakers to use for a voice amplification system due to the architecture.  You'd probably need the input and output audio threads to be exactly synchronized with the same packet size on a particular hardware platform so you can route the data through a bus list of effects in the same thread without any buffers.  (This is an experiment to try out one day.)

Calculating the actual lag between the microphone and the audio output is tricky as `AudioStreamGeneratorPlayback` only has a function [get_frames_available()](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_audiostreamgeneratorplayback.html#class-audiostreamgeneratorplayback-method-get-frames-available), but doesn't tell you the exact size of the buffer, which is often larger than the `buffer_length`.  
 
Looking at the code, the way to work out the time between the `push_buffer(audio_samples)` and when those audio_samples begin to play is:

```GDScript
    $AudioStreamGenerator.stream.mix_rate = AudioServer.get_input_mix_rate()
    var guessed_generator_buffer_frames = nearest_po2(int($AudioStreamGenerator.stream.mix_rate * $AudioStreamGenerator.stream.buffer_length))
    var buffer_time_content: float = (guessed_generator_buffer_frames - $AudioStreamGenerator.get_stream_playback().get_frames_available()) * 1.0 /$AudioStreamGenerator.stream.mix_rate
    var time_to_buffer_end = AudioServer.get_time_to_next_mix() + buffer_time_content
```

`AudioStreamGenerator` is a very interesting class from the point of view of incoming audio streams, because it's got its own buffer.  None of the other `AudioStreams` have buffers, since they pull in the data from their sources (usually an audio file) on demand in the `_mix()` function.

I think this speed and buffer management code as outlined here (where it does stuff to keep the audio buffer from under or over-flowing) for the `AudioStreamMicrophone` could work just as well in the `AudioStreamGenerator`.  Then we could use it for incoming streams (like VoIP), as well as derive the `AudioStreamMicrophone` from it to get twice the use out of this complex feature.

Assuming we output using AudioStreamGenerator (kind of irrelevant to me but yeah it accomplishes the same end) and it has fixed output buffers that are processed at a constant mix rate. It seems like the best option would be to get all available input frames, after each output buffer (assuming a double or triple buffered output scenario) finishes playing, and resampling the input frames to fit into the next output buffer. This would distort the audio frequency slightly but provide click free playback with very minimal lag (I believe).

> Assuming we output using AudioStreamGenerator (kind of irrelevant to me but yeah it accomplishes the same end) and it has fixed output buffers that are processed at a constant mix rate. It seems like the best option would be to get all available input frames, after each output buffer (assuming a double or triple buffered output scenario) finishes playing, and resampling the input frames to fit into the next output buffer. This would distort the audio frequency slightly but provide click free playback with very minimal lag (I believe).

I expect something like this idea might be the best fix. There is no perfect solution to this longstanding bug, but pops and clicks are probably going to be perceived in the majority of use cases as "worse" than distorting the audio by resampling the frequency a little bit here and there.

Edit: Also, I can test the PR once there is more agreement that it's the best solution. I'll use the same process I did in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/112836#issuecomment-3572223615 Please ping me when the dust has settled wit this PR (or another one) and I'll do another test.

To clarify my comment about looping and underrun, I'm not unhappy with how this is done. I understand the problem it's solving. But my concern is just that the same audio will be played twice due to jumping back and repeating the same data. I realize it's a rare case, but duplicated audio can be very confusing and misleading. I would suggest a simple change to fix that concern, by zeroing out the ring buffer if you happen to hit underrun. That way it will skip back and essentially fill up the buffer.

Overall I understand this is a fix of last resort, to make Godot have the best experience when it hits one of these unfortunate cases, and so we are deliberately introducing a glitch (dropping the buffer or refilling the buffer with 0's) to make the rest of the audio have no glitches.

To this regard, I am happy with this, and I think we talked about this being an ideal band aid fix in one of the audio meetings.

I just wanted to make this clarification to explain that I do agree with this change (with the fix to zero out the buffer) even though it is (by design) imperfect.

I would suggest a simple change to fix that concern, by zeroing out the ring buffer if you happen to hit underrun. That way it will skip back and essentially fill up the buffer.

So I'm not against this idea, but to reduce popping, should we fade the last sampled value to zero over a small interval of the beginning of the skip, and when the next buffer comes in fade up to the new sample at the end of the skip segment? I'm just trying to think of a way to make it less annoying to headphone users. My initial idea was that a slight echo of small segment of the last buffer would be less annoying than a couple pops, but the fade in and out of zero seems ideal (outside of just resampling everything which would be technically considerably more effort or possibly just the next step after this fix).
